questions.q: What condition must a baseline b(s) satisfy for subtracting it from the policy gradient to remain unbiased?
options: It must equal zero at every state
It must be a function of state only, not depending on the action a
It must be learned using the same network as the policy
It must always be positive
questions.explain: As long as b(s) does not depend on the action, its expected contribution to the policy gradient is provably zero, regardless of what function of state it is.

questions.q: In the proof that E[grad log(pi) * b(s)] = 0, what key fact makes the final step work?
options: The discount factor is always less than 1
The sum of action probabilities pi_theta(a|s) over all actions is always exactly 1, so its gradient with respect to theta is zero
Rewards are always non-negative
The critic network always outputs zero
questions.explain: Since probabilities must sum to 1 regardless of theta, the gradient of that constant sum is zero, which makes the whole baseline term vanish in expectation.

questions.q: What is the advantage function A(s, a)?
options: The total reward received during an episode
Q(s, a) minus V(s): how much better or worse an action is compared to the state's average value
The probability of taking action a in state s
The learning rate used by the critic
questions.explain: The advantage function subtracts the state's baseline value V(s) from the action-value Q(s,a), isolating how much better an action is than the state's average outcome.

questions.q: Why does subtracting V(s) as a baseline reduce variance in practice?
options: It removes the common component of return shared across all actions from a given state, which contributes nothing to distinguishing which action is better
It changes the expected value of the gradient to make training faster
It eliminates the need for a discount factor
It makes the policy deterministic
questions.explain: Much of a state's return variance comes from a shared component every action from that state would get anyway. Subtracting V(s) removes that shared part, leaving a tighter signal that still points toward better actions.

questions.q: How does Lesson 20's TD error, delta_t = r_t + gamma*V(s_(t+1)) - V(s_t), relate to the baseline theory in this lesson?
options: It is unrelated; the TD error is a completely different concept
It is a one-step, bootstrapped estimate of the advantage function A(s_t, a_t)
It is the same as the Monte Carlo return G_t
It eliminates the need for a baseline entirely
questions.explain: The TD error used in actor-critic methods is effectively approximating the advantage A(s,a) = Q(s,a) - V(s) using a one-step bootstrap instead of the full Q-value.
